rules.title: The HTTP WebDAV module is not installed
rules.explanation: The http_dav_module enables HTTP extensions for Web Distributed Authoring and Versioning (WebDAV), as defined in RFC 4918. WebDAV allows clients to create, delete, modify, and move files on the web server. In many modern architectures this capability has been replaced by cloud object storage or other content management approaches.
rules.impact: Unnecessary WebDAV functionality expands the attack surface of the web server. Misconfigured WebDAV operations can allow an attacker to access or manipulate files on the server.

rules.title: Gzip feature modules are disabled
rules.explanation: The http_gzip_module and related gzip directives provide HTTP response compression. Compression reduces bandwidth use but can interact with certain cryptographic attack techniques against encrypted content.
rules.impact: HTTP compression has been associated with attacks such as BREACH. Although modern HTTP usage mitigates some of these risks, disabling compression remains a defense-in-depth control against compression-related information leakage.
rules.scope: nginx build (http_gzip_module), gzip on/gzip_static on, load_module

rules.title: The autoindex module is disabled in nginx.conf
rules.explanation: The autoindex module handles requests that end with a slash by generating an automatic directory listing when no index file is present. Directory listings expose the contents of filesystem paths served by NGINX.
rules.impact: Automated directory listings can disclose naming conventions, directory structure, and files that were not intended for public access, aiding attacker reconnaissance.
rules.scope: autoindex directive in the main nginx.conf (including autoindex on)

rules.title: The autoindex module is disabled in included configurations
rules.explanation: The autoindex module handles requests that end with a slash by generating an automatic directory listing when no index file is present. Included configuration files under conf.d, sites-enabled, or snippets can re-enable this behavior independently of the main nginx.conf.
rules.impact: Automated directory listings in any included site configuration can disclose naming conventions, directory structure, and unintended files, aiding attacker reconnaissance.

rules.title: NGINX is started from a dedicated unprivileged service account without sudo privileges
rules.explanation: NGINX worker processes run under the account specified by the user directive. That service account should be dedicated to NGINX and must not hold elevated privileges such as sudo access.
rules.impact: A dedicated unprivileged service account limits the blast radius if a worker process is compromised, preventing immediate escalation through sudo or shared administrative rights.

rules.title: The NGINX worker process account exists and is not root
rules.explanation: The user directive specifies the account used for NGINX worker processes. That account must exist on the system and must not be root, so workers do not inherit full administrative privileges.
rules.impact: Running workers as root or under a missing/misconfigured account increases the impact of a process compromise and weakens isolation between the web service and the host.

rules.title: The NGINX service account is locked
rules.explanation: The NGINX service account should remain locked so it cannot authenticate with a password. If a different account runs NGINX, that account name should be substituted in audit and remediation procedures.
rules.impact: Locking the service account is a defense-in-depth control that prevents interactive login and password-based su to the NGINX user. Administrative access should use sudo instead, which does not require the service account password.

rules.title: The NGINX service account has an invalid shell
rules.explanation: The NGINX service account should not support interactive login. Its login shell should be set to a non-interactive shell such as /sbin/nologin.
rules.impact: An invalid shell restricts the account to its service role and reduces the chance that a compromised service credential can be used for interactive access to the host.

rules.title: NGINX directories and files are owned by root
rules.explanation: The /etc/nginx directory tree and its configuration files must be owned by root:root so that only privileged administrators can change web server configuration.
rules.impact: Root ownership reduces the likelihood that a non-privileged user can modify NGINX configuration and weaken security controls or introduce malicious directives.

rules.title: Access to NGINX directories is restricted
rules.explanation: Permissions on NGINX configuration directories under /etc/nginx must enforce least privilege so that unauthorized users cannot traverse or inspect configuration paths.
rules.impact: Restricting directory access limits unauthorized viewing or modification of configuration and forces privileged access (for example via sudo) for legitimate administrative work.

rules.title: Access to NGINX configuration files is restricted
rules.explanation: Permissions on NGINX configuration files under /etc/nginx must enforce least privilege so that unauthorized users cannot read or alter directives.
rules.impact: Restricted file permissions prevent unauthorized disclosure or tampering of configuration settings that control authentication, TLS, logging, and access controls.

rules.title: The NGINX PID file permissions are protected
rules.explanation: The PID file stores the process identifier of the master NGINX process, typically under a path set by the pid directive or --pid-path. Its filesystem permissions must prevent unauthorized modification.
rules.impact: World-writable or overly permissive PID file permissions can allow an attacker to replace or alter the PID value, potentially disrupting process management and contributing to denial of service.
rules.scope: PID file and parent directory permissions (pid directive / --pid-path)

rules.title: The NGINX PID file is owned by root
rules.explanation: The PID file stores the process identifier of the master NGINX process. Ownership should be root:root so that only privileged users can replace or rewrite the file.
rules.impact: Incorrect ownership of the PID file can allow unauthorized modification of the recorded process ID, which may interfere with service control and enable denial-of-service conditions.
rules.scope: Owner of the nginx PID file (/var/run/nginx.pid or --pid-path)

rules.title: NGINX listens for network connections only on authorized ports
rules.explanation: NGINX listen directives bind the server to specific IP addresses and ports. The service should listen only on ports that are authorized for the deployed application, typically including HTTP and HTTPS as required.
rules.impact: Limiting listening ports reduces unintentional service exposure and shrinks the network attack surface available to remote adversaries.
rules.scope: listen directives and actual ss/netstat sockets (80/443)

rules.title: Requests for unknown hostnames are rejected at runtime
rules.explanation: The HTTP Host header identifies the virtual host the client intends to reach and is supplied by the user agent. NGINX should accept only predefined, known-good hostnames and reject requests for unrecognized hosts.
rules.impact: Rejecting unknown Host values helps mitigate Host header injection and related attacks that redirect users to rogue hosts, execute unintended content, or harvest credentials.
rules.scope: Runtime Host-header probing (several invalid hosts, HTTP/HTTPS)

rules.title: Requests for unknown hostnames are rejected in the catch-all configuration
rules.explanation: A catch-all or default_server block handles requests that do not match a defined server_name. That block should refuse unrecognized hosts, for example by returning 444, 403, or 421, or by using a non-matching server_name such as _.
rules.impact: A properly configured catch-all prevents unintended virtual-host fallback and reduces Host header abuse that can redirect clients or serve content under an unexpected hostname.

rules.title: Keepalive_timeout is 10 seconds or less and not zero
rules.explanation: The keepalive_timeout directive limits how long an idle persistent (keep-alive) connection may remain open between the client and NGINX. Modern browsers use persistent connections to improve performance.
rules.impact: An appropriately short keep-alive timeout helps limit resource exhaustion from large numbers of idle persistent connections used in denial-of-service attacks.
rules.scope: All keepalive_timeout values with time units (s/m/ms)

rules.title: Keepalive_timeout is greater than zero
rules.explanation: The keepalive_timeout directive controls the idle lifetime of persistent HTTP connections. A value of zero disables the intended timeout behavior for keep-alive connections.
rules.impact: A non-zero keep-alive timeout ensures idle connections are closed in a controlled way, reducing the risk that long-lived connections consume server resources indefinitely.
rules.scope: All keepalive_timeout values with time units (s/m/ms)

rules.title: Send_timeout is 10 seconds or less and not zero
rules.explanation: The send_timeout directive sets the timeout between two successive write operations when sending a response to the client. It bounds how long NGINX waits during response transmission.
rules.impact: A bounded send_timeout helps mitigate slow HTTP denial-of-service techniques that hold connections open by delaying response writes and consuming worker resources.
rules.scope: All send_timeout values with time units (s/m/ms)

rules.title: Send_timeout is greater than zero
rules.explanation: The send_timeout directive sets the timeout between successive write operations when sending a response to the client. A value of zero removes that protective timeout boundary.
rules.impact: A non-zero send_timeout ensures stalled write operations are terminated, reducing exposure to slow-response denial-of-service attacks.
rules.scope: All send_timeout values with time units (s/m/ms)

rules.title: The server_tokens directive is set to off
rules.explanation: The server_tokens directive controls whether NGINX includes its version string in the Server response header and on default error pages.
rules.impact: Disabling version disclosure slows reconnaissance by reducing the information available to attackers selecting version-specific exploits.
rules.scope: server_tokens off and no version in the Server header

rules.title: The default index.html page does not reference NGINX
rules.explanation: Default welcome pages under paths such as /usr/share/nginx/html/index.html may contain branding or text that identifies NGINX as the web server software.
rules.impact: Removing NGINX identifiers from default pages reduces technology fingerprinting and can lower the likelihood of targeted attacks against known NGINX deployments.

rules.title: The default 50x.html error page does not reference NGINX
rules.explanation: Default error pages such as /usr/share/nginx/html/50x.html may disclose that the site is served by NGINX through branding or explicit product references.
rules.impact: Removing NGINX identifiers from error pages reduces technology fingerprinting useful to attackers during reconnaissance.

rules.title: Transfer of hidden files is disabled
rules.explanation: Hidden files and directories (names beginning with a dot, such as .git) can contain sensitive metadata or credentials. NGINX location matching can deny requests for these paths as a defense-in-depth measure.
rules.impact: Blocking access to hidden files reduces the risk that an attacker retrieves sensitive content that was inadvertently placed under the document root or application tree.
rules.scope: location block ~ /\. with deny all or return 403/404/444

rules.title: The NGINX reverse proxy does not disclose the X-Powered-By header
rules.explanation: When NGINX acts as a reverse proxy, upstream applications may return an X-Powered-By header that identifies frameworks or runtimes. Directives such as proxy_hide_header or more_clear_headers can suppress this header.
rules.impact: Hiding technology-identifying headers reduces the effectiveness of automated reconnaissance against the upstream stack.

rules.title: The NGINX reverse proxy does not disclose the upstream Server header
rules.explanation: When NGINX acts as a reverse proxy, upstream servers may return their own Server header. Directives such as proxy_hide_header or more_clear_headers can prevent that upstream Server header from being passed to clients.
rules.impact: Suppressing upstream Server headers limits disclosure of backend software versions and reduces reconnaissance value for attackers.

rules.title: Verbose access logging is enabled
rules.explanation: A detailed log_format captures useful request metadata such as client address, timestamp, request line, status, bytes sent, and User-Agent. Logging should follow organizational security and privacy policy and avoid recording sensitive data in query strings or URIs.
rules.impact: Verbose access logs support incident response, auditing, and forensic investigation by preserving who accessed what and when. Insufficient detail impedes detection and reconstruction of security events.

rules.title: Access logging is enabled
rules.explanation: The access_log directive records client requests for each site. Access logging is enabled by default in typical NGINX builds but can be disabled per server or location.
rules.impact: Access logs allow incident responders and auditors to investigate who accessed the service and which resources were requested during an incident.

rules.title: Error logging is enabled at the info level or higher
rules.explanation: The error_log directive records NGINX and application-related errors. Configuring the severity to info (or a more verbose level such as debug where appropriate) captures operational and security-relevant events.
rules.impact: Error logs help identify attacks and application issues. An info-level (or higher) configuration provides enough detail for investigation while supporting detection of abnormal behavior.
rules.scope: error_log with info or debug level

rules.title: Log files are rotated on a defined schedule
rules.explanation: Log rotation (for example via /etc/logrotate.d/nginx on a daily or weekly schedule) archives and replaces active log files so they do not grow without bound.
rules.impact: Without scheduled rotation, logs can fill disk space and cause denial of service when logging or other services can no longer write to disk.

rules.title: Log rotation retains a defined number of archives
rules.explanation: Logrotate rotate settings control how many archived copies of NGINX logs are retained, often with options such as compress, missingok, and postrotate hooks to signal NGINX.
rules.impact: Retaining a bounded number of rotated archives preserves investigative history while preventing unbounded disk consumption that could interrupt logging availability.

rules.title: Error logs are sent to a remote syslog server
rules.explanation: NGINX can send error_log output to a remote syslog destination so that events are stored outside the local host. Centralized logging supports audit and incident investigation.
rules.impact: Remote aggregation preserves log availability if the web server is compromised or wiped, and enables correlation of events across systems for attack detection and forensic use.
rules.scope: error_log syslog directive in the nginx configuration

rules.title: Access logs are sent to a remote syslog server
rules.explanation: NGINX can send access_log output to a remote syslog destination so that request history is stored outside the local host. Centralized logging supports audit and incident investigation.
rules.impact: Remote access-log aggregation preserves evidence if the local host is compromised and supports correlation of client activity across systems during an incident.
rules.scope: access_log syslog directive in the nginx configuration

rules.title: The NGINX reverse proxy is configured to forward client requests
rules.explanation: When NGINX operates as a reverse proxy, proxy_pass directs client requests to upstream application servers. Correct proxy configuration is a prerequisite for preserving client identity headers toward those backends.
rules.impact: A properly configured reverse proxy path enables controlled forwarding of traffic and supports accurate logging and access decisions based on the original client identity.

rules.title: Proxies forward the client address via X-Real-IP
rules.explanation: The X-Real-IP request header commonly carries the original client IP address when NGINX proxies to an upstream. The proxy_set_header X-Real-IP directive populates this header for backend applications and logs.
rules.impact: Preserving the original client IP helps auditors and incident responders attribute activity, support blocking decisions, and correlate attacker behavior across tiers.

rules.title: Proxies forward the client address via X-Forwarded-For
rules.explanation: The X-Forwarded-For header records the originating client address and any intermediate proxy addresses as requests traverse reverse proxies. The proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For directive forwards this information to upstream servers.
rules.impact: Accurate forwarding of client address information supports attribution, rate limiting, and forensic correlation when investigating abuse or attacks through the proxy path.

rules.title: A trusted certificate and trust chain are installed
rules.explanation: TLS certificates and their intermediate chain of trust allow clients to verify that the web server identity matches the presented certificate. Certificate authorities validate domain control as part of issuance.
rules.impact: Without a valid certificate and complete trust chain, modern browsers and clients treat the site as untrusted, undermining encrypted communications and user confidence.
rules.scope: ssl_certificate: openssl subject, validity period, file readability

rules.title: Private key permissions are restricted
rules.explanation: The TLS private key referenced by ssl_certificate_key must be protected according to least privilege. Typical hardened modes include 400, 440, or 600 with ownership limited to root or the service account that must read the key.
rules.impact: An unprotected private key can be copied by an unauthorized local user and used to decrypt TLS traffic or impersonate the server, defeating confidentiality and authenticity guarantees.

rules.title: Only modern TLS protocols are enabled
rules.explanation: The ssl_protocols directive selects the TLS protocol versions offered to clients. Modern deployments should enable TLS 1.2 and/or TLS 1.3, which provide contemporary cryptographic capabilities.
rules.impact: TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3 support stronger cipher suites, forward secrecy, and authenticated encryption. Relying on these versions protects users who negotiate the highest mutually supported secure protocol.

rules.title: Legacy TLS and SSL protocols are disabled
rules.explanation: Obsolete protocols such as SSL 3.0, TLS 1.0, and TLS 1.1 lack modern protections and should be removed from ssl_protocols. Only current TLS versions should remain available for client and upstream connections.
rules.impact: Legacy protocols enable known weaknesses (for example POODLE against SSL 3.0) and fail modern compliance expectations such as PCI DSS restrictions on TLS 1.0. Disabling them prevents negotiation of insecure stacks.
rules.scope: ssl_protocols without SSLv2/3, TLSv1, TLSv1.0, TLSv1.1

rules.title: Weak ciphers are disabled in ssl_ciphers
rules.explanation: The ssl_ciphers directive defines the cipher suites offered to TLS clients. Weak or obsolete suites should be excluded per organizational policy or industry baselines, and ssl_prefer_server_ciphers should prefer the server's cipher order.
rules.impact: Strong server-enforced ciphers protect confidentiality and integrity of TLS sessions. Weak suites allow outdated clients to negotiate vulnerable cryptography and increase exposure to protocol-level attacks.
rules.scope: ssl_ciphers without weak tokens + ssl_prefer_server_ciphers on

rules.title: Weak ciphers are disabled in proxy_ssl_ciphers
rules.explanation: The proxy_ssl_ciphers directive defines cipher suites used when NGINX establishes TLS connections to upstream servers. Weak suites should be excluded so upstream encryption meets the same strength as client-facing TLS.
rules.impact: Weak upstream ciphers can undermine end-to-end security when a reverse proxy or load balancer is in use, allowing vulnerable negotiation on the backend path even if client TLS is strong.
rules.scope: proxy_ssl_ciphers for HTTPS upstream without weak tokens

rules.title: Custom Diffie-Hellman parameters are used
rules.explanation: The ssl_dhparam directive points NGINX to a Diffie-Hellman parameter file used with ephemeral DH (DHE) key exchange. Custom parameters of at least 2048 bits should be generated rather than relying on weak defaults.
rules.impact: Strong, unique DH parameters improve Perfect Forward Secrecy for compatible cipher suites. Default 1024-bit parameters provide weaker protection for recorded traffic if long-term keys are later compromised.
rules.scope: ssl_dhparam file and parameter length >= 2048 bits

rules.title: OCSP stapling is enabled
rules.explanation: OCSP stapling (ssl_stapling) allows NGINX to attach a recent Online Certificate Status Protocol response to the TLS handshake so clients can check revocation status without a separate OCSP query in many cases.
rules.impact: Stapling improves revocation checking reliability and privacy for clients and helps them detect revoked certificates more efficiently during the handshake.

rules.title: OCSP stapling verification is enabled
rules.explanation: The ssl_stapling_verify directive instructs NGINX to verify OCSP responses before stapling them. It complements ssl_stapling and typically relies on trusted CA material such as ssl_trusted_certificate.
rules.impact: Verifying stapled OCSP responses reduces the risk that forged or invalid revocation status is presented to clients.

rules.title: HTTP Strict Transport Security (HSTS) is enabled
rules.explanation: The Strict-Transport-Security response header tells compliant user agents to interact with the host only over HTTPS for a defined max-age. Effective HSTS commonly uses a long max-age (at least six months), the always flag, and includeSubDomains where appropriate.
rules.impact: HSTS reduces the risk of protocol downgrade and SSL-stripping attacks by ensuring browsers refuse cleartext access after the policy is observed.

rules.title: Upstream server traffic is authenticated with a client certificate
rules.explanation: When NGINX proxies over HTTPS, proxy_ssl_certificate and proxy_ssl_certificate_key present a client certificate to the upstream so the backend can authenticate the proxy.
rules.impact: Mutual TLS authentication with upstream servers reduces the risk that unauthorized intermediaries can establish trusted connections to backend applications.
rules.scope: proxy_ssl_certificate and proxy_ssl_certificate_key for HTTPS upstream

rules.title: The upstream server certificate is trusted via proxy_ssl_trusted_certificate
rules.explanation: The proxy_ssl_trusted_certificate directive provides the CA certificates NGINX uses to validate upstream TLS certificates when connecting to backend servers.
rules.impact: Trusting only expected upstream certificate authorities reduces the risk of man-in-the-middle attacks between NGINX and backend services.

rules.title: Upstream TLS certificate verification is enabled
rules.explanation: The proxy_ssl_verify directive enables verification of the upstream server certificate when NGINX opens a TLS connection to a backend. Verification should be turned on for HTTPS upstreams.
rules.impact: Without upstream certificate verification, NGINX may accept forged or unexpected backend identities, enabling man-in-the-middle attacks on proxied traffic.

rules.title: TLS session tickets are disabled to preserve perfect forward secrecy
rules.explanation: The ssl_session_tickets directive controls use of TLS session tickets for session resumption. Disabling session tickets avoids shared ticket-encryption keys that can weaken forward secrecy properties.
rules.impact: Session ticket keys that are long-lived or shared can allow decryption of resumed sessions if the ticket key is compromised, expanding the impact of a key disclosure beyond a single connection.

rules.title: HTTP/2 is used
rules.explanation: HTTP/2 is a multiplexed successor to HTTP/1.1 that can be enabled on TLS listeners via the http2 listen parameter or the http2 directive. Some legacy user agents may not support HTTP/2.
rules.impact: HTTP/2 improves performance through multiplexing and strengthens the security posture by aligning with modern TLS expectations, disabling TLS renegotiation and compression, and tightening cipher requirements relative to older HTTP stacks.
rules.scope: http2 parameter in listen / http2 directive

rules.title: Only Perfect Forward Secrecy ciphers are used
rules.explanation: Perfect Forward Secrecy (PFS) cipher suites use ephemeral key exchange such as ECDHE or DHE. The ssl_ciphers and proxy_ssl_ciphers settings should exclude static key-exchange suites that lack PFS.
rules.impact: PFS ensures that compromise of the server's long-term private key does not allow decryption of previously recorded TLS sessions negotiated with ephemeral key exchange.

rules.title: Allow and deny filters restrict access to approved IP addresses
rules.explanation: NGINX allow and deny directives implement IP-based access control. Configurations should permit only trusted addresses and apply a default deny in accordance with organizational policy.
rules.impact: IP allowlisting reduces the exposed attack surface and helps prevent unauthorized access to administrative interfaces or other sensitive locations.
rules.scope: allow; deny all directives as default deny

rules.title: Deny filters block unauthorized IP addresses
rules.explanation: NGINX deny directives explicitly refuse connections from specified addresses or networks. A default deny all closing rule is commonly used with preceding allow entries.
rules.impact: Explicit deny rules help block untrusted or known-malicious sources and reinforce least-privilege access to sensitive resources.
rules.scope: deny directives, presence of deny all

rules.title: Only approved HTTP methods are allowed
rules.explanation: HTTP methods (verbs) request specific actions on a resource path. NGINX can restrict methods with constructs such as limit_except or request_method checks so that only necessary verbs are accepted.
rules.impact: Most sites require only GET, POST, and HEAD. Allowing unused methods expands the attack surface; restricting verbs to those required by the application reduces unnecessary risk.

rules.title: Client header and body read timeouts are set correctly
rules.explanation: The client_header_timeout and client_body_timeout directives limit how long NGINX waits while reading the client request header and body, respectively.
rules.impact: Bounded client read timeouts help mitigate Slowloris-style and other slow-request denial-of-service attacks that hold connections open by sending data very slowly.

rules.title: The maximum request body size is set correctly
rules.explanation: The client_max_body_size directive limits the size of the client request body, corresponding to the Content-Length of the request. A non-zero explicit limit should be set appropriately for the application.
rules.impact: Limiting request body size reduces the risk of resource exhaustion and overly large payloads being passed to applications, while still allowing legitimate uploads within defined bounds.
rules.scope: client_max_body_size is explicitly set and is not 0

rules.title: The maximum URI buffer size is defined
rules.explanation: The large_client_header_buffers directive sets the number and size of buffers used to read large client request headers, including long URIs. Typical hardening starts around two buffers of 1 KB each, adjusted for application needs.
rules.impact: Bounding large header buffers helps mitigate attacks that use oversized request lines or headers to consume memory or trigger buffer-related failures.

rules.title: Connections per IP address are limited with limit_conn_zone
rules.explanation: The limit_conn_zone directive in the http context defines a shared memory zone keyed by client address (for example $binary_remote_addr) to track concurrent connections for later limit_conn use.
rules.impact: Connection accounting per IP supports enforcement of concurrency limits that mitigate slow denial-of-service and some brute-force patterns that open many simultaneous connections.

rules.title: Connections per IP address are limited with limit_conn
rules.explanation: The limit_conn directive in server or location contexts applies a maximum number of simultaneous connections for a previously defined limit_conn_zone, typically keyed by client IP address.
rules.impact: Enforcing per-IP connection limits reduces resource exhaustion from many concurrent connections and can slow brute-force attempts against exposed login or API endpoints.

rules.title: Per-IP rate limits are configured with limit_req_zone
rules.explanation: The limit_req_zone directive in the http context defines a shared memory zone and request rate (rate=) keyed by client address for use with limit_req. Thresholds should match application needs and organizational policy.
rules.impact: Request-rate zones enable controlled throttling that helps mitigate flooding and certain denial-of-service patterns as a defense-in-depth measure.
rules.scope: limit_req_zone with rate= and a client address key

rules.title: Per-IP rate limits are configured with limit_req
rules.explanation: The limit_req directive in server or location contexts applies the request-rate policy defined by a limit_req_zone, restricting how quickly a single client address may issue requests.
rules.impact: Applying per-IP rate limits reduces the effectiveness of request floods and abusive automation targeting specific locations or virtual hosts.

rules.title: The X-Frame-Options header is configured and enabled
rules.explanation: The X-Frame-Options response header controls whether a browser may embed the response in a frame or iframe. Common values are DENY or SAMEORIGIN, applied with add_header and typically the always flag.
rules.impact: Restricting framing reduces the risk of clickjacking attacks that overlay or embed the site to trick users into unintended actions.

rules.title: The X-Content-Type-Options header is configured and enabled
rules.explanation: The X-Content-Type-Options header with the nosniff value instructs browsers not to MIME-sniff responses away from the declared Content-Type. It is commonly set with add_header and the always flag.
rules.impact: Disabling MIME sniffing reduces content-type confusion attacks in which a browser interprets a response as executable or otherwise unintended content.

rules.title: Content-Security-Policy is enabled and configured correctly
rules.explanation: The Content-Security-Policy (CSP) response header restricts the sources from which the browser may load executable and other content, commonly beginning with a default-src directive applied via add_header.
rules.impact: A correctly scoped CSP reduces the impact of cross-site scripting and other content injection by limiting where scripts and related resources may originate.

rules.title: Referrer-Policy is enabled and configured correctly
rules.explanation: The Referrer-Policy response header controls how much referrer information the browser sends with subsequent requests. Values such as no-referrer or strict-origin are selected according to organizational policy.
rules.impact: A restrictive referrer policy reduces leakage of sensitive URL paths and query data to third parties when users navigate away from the site.
